title: Area V review: IFR Operating Rules
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area V: flight plans, alternates and fuel; takeoff, approach and landing minimums; reports and lost communications; and equipment checks and databases. Many join two of them in one IFR flight, the way an IPC instructor would ask.

questions.q: An alternate is required. With the forecast winds aloft, you need 2+10 to the destination and 0+30 more to the alternate. Normal cruise burns 9.5 GPH, and you have 34 gallons usable. Ignoring taxi and climb, what does 91.167 require?
options: About 32.5 gallons, so your 34 gallons are legal with about 1.5 to spare
About 27.7 gallons: the destination plus 45 minutes, since the alternate leg comes out of the reserve
About 25.3 gallons: the destination and the alternate, since the 45 minutes is a VFR night rule
About 34.8 gallons: IFR needs 1 hour after the alternate, so 34 gallons is not enough
questions.why: 91.167 counts weather reports and forecasts, so the forecast winds set the times [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]]. Then it adds the leg to the alternate and 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2), (3)]]. 2:10 + 0:30 + 0:45 = 3:25, or 3.417 hours; 3.417 x 9.5 = 32.46 gallons. The 45 minutes comes after the alternate, not in place of it. It is not borrowed from the VFR night rule, which is a separate rule [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]], and no rule asks for a full hour.

questions.q: On an IFR flight plan to a nontowered airport, your only comm radio fails in VFR conditions 15 NM out. You continue VFR and land there. What is still required?
options: Nothing: squawking 7600 closed the IFR flight plan
Tell an FSS or ATC facility that the flight is complete, for example by telephone after landing
Nothing: ATC closes the plan when your target leaves radar
Nothing more, but you should have stayed IFR to a towered airport so the tower would close the plan
questions.why: In VFR conditions after a radio failure you continue VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]], so staying IFR to a towered field is the wrong choice. A plan closes by itself on landing only at a field with a working tower. At a nontowered field the pilot must start the cancellation, and the AIM mentions doing it by telephone [[33:340|AIM 5-1-15e, f]]. 91.169(d) requires telling an FSS or ATC facility when you cancel or complete the flight [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(d)]]. Code 7600 only signals the radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]].

questions.q: Your only approach navigator is a WAAS GPS (TSO-C146). The planned alternate has one approach, an RNAV (GPS) with LPV and LNAV lines, no A or A NA symbol and no negative W. The forecast there at your ETA is 700 ft overcast and 3 SM. Does it qualify as your alternate?
options: No: you must plan on the LNAV line with Part 91 nonprecision weather, 800 ft and 2 SM, and 700 ft is below it
Yes: LPV has vertical guidance, so the 600 ft and 2 SM precision value applies
Yes: with WAAS, any forecast at or above the LPV DA and visibility qualifies
No: an airport whose only approach is GPS can never be listed as an alternate
questions.why: With WAAS at an alternate, planning must use the LNAV or circling line, with Part 91 nonprecision weather [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18c]]. With no nonstandard minimums listed, that is 800 ft and 2 SM [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]], so 700 ft fails. LPV may be used only once you arrive and the receiver shows it available [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18c]]. The rule against a GPS-only alternate does not apply to WAAS equipment [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3d]], so the last choice is wrong.

questions.q: Your ETA is 1615Z at a destination with an ILS. The forecast: until 1700Z, overcast 3,000 ft above the airport and 5 SM; from 1700Z, overcast 1,500 ft and 3 SM. Do you need an alternate?
options: No: at the 1615Z ETA the ceiling is 3,000 ft
No: 1,500 ft is still above the 600 ft standard alternate minimum for an ILS
Only if the visibility also drops below 3 SM after 1700Z
Yes: the test runs from 1515Z to 1715Z, and from 1700Z the ceiling is below 2,000 ft
questions.why: To skip the alternate, the ceiling must be at least 2,000 ft above the airport and the visibility at least 3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)(2)(i)]]. Here that window is 1515Z to 1715Z, and the 1,500 ft ceiling from 1700Z falls inside it. One item short is enough; the visibility need not fail too. The 600 ft figure is an alternate minimum, used to judge the alternate, not the destination [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]]. The fuel must now cover the alternate leg as well [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)]].

questions.q: In IMC at a nontowered field you get: "Cleared to Lakeport as filed, climb and maintain 6,000, clearance void if not off by 1420." Your runway has a textual ODP. The clearance names no ODP, SID or headings. You fly Part 91. What is right?
options: The ODP is mandatory for any IFR departure from that runway because it is published
Once departure says "radar contact", ATC is responsible for your obstacle clearance
Obstacle clearance is yours; flying the ODP is your choice and is encouraged in IMC, and you should tell ATC if you use it; be airborne by 1420
You may not fly the ODP, because it is not in your clearance
questions.why: A void time lets you depart only within that period [[23:298|IFH 10-7]]. The 91.175(f) duty to use a published ODP binds Parts 121, 125, 129 and 135, not Part 91 [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(f)]]. Departing Part 91 without an ODP, SID or DVA headings in the clearance, obstacle clearance is the pilot's job, and "radar contact" does not change that [[33:354|AIM 5-2-9f]]. An ODP may be flown without a clearance unless ATC assigned a SID or vectors, and Part 91 pilots are strongly encouraged to fly one in IMC [[33:349|AIM 5-2-9a, c]]. If you use it, inform ATC [[29:39|IPH 1-23]].

questions.q: After a missed approach at the destination you divert to your alternate. You listed it using the standard 600 ft and 2 SM for its ILS. The ILS line shows a DA 200 ft above touchdown and 1/2 SM. Which numbers govern the approach you now fly there?
options: 600 ft and 2 SM, the minimums you planned with
800 ft and 2 SM, because it is an alternate
The ILS DA and visibility on the chart, raised only if a 91.175(b) item such as your equipment needs a higher one
The forecast you used at your ETA there
questions.why: Alternate minimums decide only whether you may list an airport as an alternate, by comparing them with the forecast at your ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(c)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)]]. The approach you fly follows 91.175, where the authorized DA is the highest of the procedure, the pilot's and the equipment's [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(a), (b)]]. The AIM shows the same split for WAAS: plan on LNAV, but on arrival use LPV if it is available [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18c]]. Report the missed approach and ask for a clearance to the alternate [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(d)]].

questions.q: Your ILS chart shows an ALSF-2. At the DA you see the approach lights, but no red bars beside or at the end of them, and nothing else yet. The flight visibility meets the chart value and a normal descent works. What may you do?
options: Continue to touchdown: the approach light system is one of the listed references
Continue below 100 ft above the TDZE, since the flight visibility meets the chart value
Go missed at the DA: approach lights alone never let you go below a DA
Continue, but not below 100 ft above TDZE unless red terminating or side row bars, or another listed reference, come into view
questions.why: The approach lights are a valid reference for leaving the DA, but with only them in sight you may not go below 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also distinctly visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]. A civil ALSF-2 may be run as an SSALR in good weather, and the SSALR drawing shows no red lights [[33:122|AIM FIG 2-1-1]]. So an ALSF-2 on the chart does not promise red bars tonight. If no other reference appears by 100 ft above TDZE, go missed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. The limit is 100 ft above TDZE, not a margin below the DA, and it holds for any DA height.

questions.q: On vectors for an ILS in IMC, in controlled airspace, the glideslope flag appears and stays. The localizer works. The chart has ILS and LOC lines of minimums. What do the rules require?
options: Tell ATC the glideslope has failed, how that limits you and what you want, and use the LOC minimums
Fly the ILS DA on the localizer alone, since the procedure lists that DA
No report: 91.187 covers only a complete loss of the ILS receiver
Report it, but keep the ILS minimums, because the failure is in the airplane, not on the ground
questions.why: The authorized DA or MDA is the highest of the procedure's, the pilot's and the one for the equipment available and used [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]]. With the glideslope out, the localizer minimums apply [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]; for a failed receiver in the airplane, that follows from the equipment item of 91.175(b). 91.187 requires a report of any nav or approach equipment malfunction, with identification, equipment, degree of impairment and assistance wanted [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. The AIM lists partial loss of ILS receiver capability as reportable [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]].

questions.q: Your IFR route in Class E airspace has one airway segment with an MEA of 10,500 and no MOCA. The airplane's altimeter and encoder test entry reads "tested to 10,000 ft." What can you do?
options: Fly that segment at 10,000: the MEA gives way when the altimeter test limits you
Re-plan on a route whose minimum IFR altitudes let you stay at or below 10,000, or have the system tested higher
Fly it at 11,000: the tested altitude limits only the encoder's reports
Ask for a VFR-on-top clearance at 10,500, which is not limited by these rules
questions.why: Below the MEA is not allowed except for takeoff or landing, or where a MOCA lets you descend [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. Above 10,000 is not allowed either: no IFR in controlled airspace above the highest altitude to which all altimeters and the encoder were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]]. The minimum altitude rules apply to every IFR flight, VFR-on-top included [[29:95|IPH 2-35]]. So that segment cannot be flown legally, and the fix is a new route or a new test.

questions.q: Your LOC approach requires RVR 4000. RVR is not reported for your runway, and the tower reports 1 SM. Level at the MDA past the VDP, you see the runway lights, but you judge the flight visibility to be about 1/2 SM. What applies?
options: Land: the reported 1 SM is above the required value
Land: RVR 4000 converts to 1/2 SM
You may not land: RVR 4000 converts to 3/4 SM, and the flight visibility you judge is below it
You may not even fly the approach: with RVR unreported, an RVR minimum cannot be used
questions.why: When RVR is prescribed but not reported, you convert it with the 91.175(h) table [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(h)(1)]], and RVR 4000 equals 3/4 SM [[60:474|14 CFR 91.175(h)(2)]]. You may not go below the MDA, or land, when the flight visibility is less than the visibility the approach prescribes [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c), (d)]]. The report does not decide it: only the pilot can judge flight visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. Go missed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)]].

questions.q: Your airplane's VREF at maximum landing weight is 85 knots. In strong, gusty winds you plan to fly the final of a straight-in approach at 100 knots. According to the AIM, which minimums should you use?
options: Category A: VREF at maximum landing weight sets the category, and the speed you fly does not change it
Category B
Category C
The lowest line shown, since a straight-in is not a circle
questions.why: The category comes from VREF, or 1.3 VSO, at maximum certified landing weight, so this airplane is Category A, below 91 knots [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7a]] [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7e]]. But if you must fly faster than the upper limit of your category's speed range, the AIM says to use the higher category's minimums, and it names heavy or gusty wind as a case; its straight-in example is a Category A airplane at 130 knots using Category C [[33:422|AIM 5-4-7b]]. 100 knots is in the Category B range of 91 knots or more but less than 121 [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7e]], not Category C.

questions.q: Circling at the MDA to land on runway 27 after an approach to runway 9, a rain shower hides the airport on downwind. It is not just your bank. What do you do?
options: Go missed now: start a climbing turn toward the landing runway and join the missed approach for the approach you flew
Hold the MDA and keep circling until the airport shows again
Descend below the MDA to get under the shower
Turn back to the final course and fly to the MAP before you climb
questions.why: When an identifiable part of the airport is not distinctly visible while circling, for any reason other than a normal bank, you must go missed immediately [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)]]. Fly the missed approach for that procedure, with an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway to get onto the missed course [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]. Waiting or going back to the MAP delays a required missed approach. A missed started while circling may not keep you clear of obstacles, so climb without delay [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]].

questions.q: Center says: "Fly heading 120, radar vectors to the HOTEL VOR, maintain 4,000." Your radios then fail in IMC. The direct line from your position to HOTEL is off airways and outside any mountainous area, and no minimum altitude is published for it. The highest obstacle within 4 NM of that line is a tower whose top is 3,620 ft MSL. No altitude was given to expect. What do you fly?
options: Hold heading 120 at 4,000 until ATC finds you on radar
Direct to HOTEL at no lower than 4,620 ft, the higher of 4,000 and the 91.177 minimum for that leg
Direct to HOTEL at 4,000: ATC assigned it, and it is at or above the MVA
Back to your filed route at its MEA, since vectors are not a route
questions.why: Being vectored, the 91.185 route is direct from the point of failure to the fix named in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(ii)]]. The altitude is the highest of the assigned altitude, the minimum altitude for IFR operations and any expected altitude [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]. With no minimum published in Parts 95 and 97, 91.177 sets it at 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course: 3,620 + 1,000 = 4,620 ft, which is higher than 4,000 [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)]]. 91.177 does not list an MVA. MVAs are set for ATC to use when vectoring, and some are lower than the charted minimum altitudes [[33:411|AIM 5-4-5e]], so the 4,000 ft vector altitude does not settle this leg.

questions.q: You fly IFR in IMC in controlled airspace. Your navigator is a WAAS GPS (TSO-C146). You also have one VOR receiver, which you are not using. It fails. What does the rule require?
options: Nothing: a Part 91 WAAS user needs no VOR, so nothing that matters has failed
Report it only if ATC later asks you to fly a VOR approach
Report it to ATC as soon as practical: identification, the VOR receiver, how much it limits you, and any help you want
Squawk 7600 and follow 91.185
questions.why: 91.187 requires a report of any malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment in flight, with four items in order, and it is not limited to equipment the flight needs [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. The AIM lists loss of VOR receiver capability [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]]. Part 91 WAAS users need not carry VOR avionics [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3f]]. That changes item 3, how much you are impaired, not whether you report. Code 7600 is for two-way radio failure [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2a]].

questions.q: Your clearance: "Cleared to the BRAVO VOR via V22, maintain 7,000. Expect further clearance via V44 to Kent at 1530." BRAVO is not a fix where an approach begins. The radios fail in IMC before BRAVO, and you reach BRAVO at 1512. What does 91.185 say?
options: Leave BRAVO on arrival at 1512 and fly your filed route to Kent
Hold at BRAVO until 1530, then fly V44 to a fix where a Kent approach begins, and start the approach as close as possible to your ETA
Hold at BRAVO until 1530, then begin an approach from BRAVO
Leave BRAVO on arrival and fly V44, since the EFC no longer counts once the radios fail
questions.why: Fly the assigned route, V22, to BRAVO [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(i)]]. Beyond BRAVO you have no assigned route, so you fly the route ATC said to expect, V44. The filed route is used only when there is neither [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)(iii), (iv)]]. A clearance limit that is not an approach fix is left at the EFC, here 1530. You then go to a fix where an approach begins and start down as close as possible to the ETA from your filed or amended ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(ii)]]. Waiting at BRAVO until 1530 means holding there; that part is application.

questions.q: Ten miles before CEDAR, Center says: "Bonanza 345KT, contact Approach 124.3 at CEDAR." What does the AIM expect?
options: Switch to Approach now and check in, to be early on the new frequency
Acknowledge, then listen on 124.3 and wait for Approach to call you
Switch at CEDAR without acknowledging, to keep the frequency clear
Acknowledge, keep a listening watch on Center until CEDAR, then switch and check in with your altitude
questions.why: Keep a listening watch on the transferring controller's frequency until the time, fix or altitude given [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b1]]. Acknowledge the call; without that, the controller cannot tell whether you got it [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d]]. On first contact with a radar controller, give your assigned altitude with "level", or your altitude while climbing or descending [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1b2(a)]]. 91.183 requires a continuous watch on the appropriate frequency [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]]. Until CEDAR, that is Center.

questions.q: Level at your assigned 6,000 ft with the current altimeter setting, Center says: "Verify at 6,000. Your Mode C shows 6,300." What do you do?
options: Descend 300 ft so the readout shows 6,000
Turn the transponder off on your own to stop the wrong readout
Say nothing and stay at 6,000, since the controller has not changed your altitude
Tell Center you are level at 6,000, your assigned altitude, and keep it unless the controller authorizes a change
questions.why: Asked to verify an altitude, confirm it or tell the controller the altitude you are actually holding, and do not change altitude to match unless the controller specifically authorizes it [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1b3]]. Staying silent skips the reply the AIM asks for. In controlled airspace you must keep the transponder on, with Mode C if installed, unless ATC directs otherwise [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]], and Mode C is deactivated only when ATC directs it [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217(a)]]. A 300 ft gap is also more than the 125 ft the encoder is calibrated to [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217(a)]], which points at the system, not your flying.

questions.q: You fly a TSO-C129 GPS with FDE and have the needed training and one VOR receiver. The RAIM prediction at the destination is good, and you will fly the RNAV (GPS) approach there. An alternate is required. Airport X has only an RNAV (GPS) approach. Airport Y has only a VOR approach. Both forecasts are above their alternate minimums. Which plan is legal?
options: List Y: its VOR approach does not rely on GPS, and the airplane has the VOR receiver to fly it
List X on its LNAV line, since FDE and a RAIM prediction allow GPS planning at the alternate
List Y, but only if the destination also has a non-GPS approach you could plan on
List neither: a non-WAAS GPS user may not plan a GPS approach at the destination when an alternate is required
questions.why: With FDE, a RAIM prediction and the training, a TSO-C129 user may plan a GPS-based approach at the destination or at the alternate, but not at both [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3d]] [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(c)]]. The destination uses it, so the alternate needs an approved approach other than GPS that should be working at your ETA and that the airplane is equipped to fly [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3d]] [[33:95|AIM 1-1-17b5(d)]]. That rules out X. Y qualifies with your VOR receiver, which also covers the rule that a non-WAAS user has the avionics for the ground facilities at the destination and the alternate [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17b3(b)]]. The destination does not need a second, non-GPS approach, and GPS is allowed at the destination.

questions.q: Your GPS database expired October 1, 2026, and you cannot update it today. The destination RNAV (GPS) chart reads "Amdt 4 01OCT26". The ILS there has its glideslope out by NOTAM. What is the plan?
options: Fly the RNAV (GPS) from the database after checking that its waypoints look logical
Fly the RNAV (GPS) on the LNAV line, since only LPV needs a current database
Fly the ILS to its normal DA, since a ground glideslope outage does not change the minimums
Do not fly the RNAV (GPS) from this database; plan the localizer approach with localizer minimums
questions.why: If a procedure's amendment date is on or after the database expiration date, you must not use the database to fly it [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3 Note 4]]. The date after "Amdt" is when the change took effect [[2:100|Chart Users' Guide p 100]]. A logical-looking waypoint check is the en route rule, and an approach needs a current database or proof the procedure was not amended [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]]. That covers every line, LNAV too. With the glideslope out, localizer minimums apply [[23:313|IFH 10-22]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(b)]].

questions.q: On September 20 you checked your two independent VOR receivers against each other on the same station: 3 degrees apart. You logged the date, place, "3 degrees" and signed. Today, October 24, you plan IFR on Victor airways. What is true?
options: Good: a VOR check lasts through the end of the next calendar month
Not good today: the check is 34 days old, and 91.171 needs one within the preceding 30 days
Not good: 3 degrees is over the dual check limit
Not good: a dual check counts only if it was made in flight
questions.why: A dual system check is allowed in place of the other methods, with up to 4 degrees between the two, so 3 degrees passed [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. The record was complete: date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. But the rule counts days, not calendar months: within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. From September 20 to October 24 is 34 days. Nothing in 91.171(c) requires the dual check to be made in flight.

questions.q: Descending on the LNAV line 1 NM past the final approach waypoint, your non-WAAS GPS shows a RAIM flag. The runway is not yet in sight. What do you do?
options: Continue to the MDA and VDP, since the position was good at the waypoint
Stay level, fly to the missed approach waypoint, then go missed
Start a climb and fly the missed approach, treating the GPS guidance as advisory only
Keep descending on the displayed course, since the receiver still shows guidance
questions.why: If the RAIM flag appears after the FAWP, start a climb and fly the missed approach; the GPS information may keep showing but is advisory only [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)]]. Flying on to the MAWP before going missed is the AIM's procedure for a flag before the FAWP [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)]]. Continuing down on guidance the AIM calls advisory only has no integrity behind it. Then report the missed approach and ask for what you want next [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(d)]].

questions.q: Your non-turbine single has no MEL. Its gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator has failed, and there is no third attitude system. Tomorrow's flight is IFR in IMC. What is true?
options: No IFR until it is fixed; for a VFR flight it may be deferred if every 91.213(d) condition is met
You may fly IFR once it is placarded inoperative under 91.213(d)
You may fly IFR, because the attitude indicator shows the same bank information
You may fly IFR by day only, because it is a night item
questions.why: 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator for IFR, unless the airplane has an approved third attitude system usable through 360 degrees of pitch and roll [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Required items must be operable [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]. 91.213(d) cannot defer an item that 91.205 requires for the kind of flight you are making [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. So it grounds the airplane for IFR. For VFR it is not on the 91.205 list, so deferral may be possible if the other conditions are met.

questions.q: The airplane's 91.411 test is 8 months old. Last week a shop replaced a cracked static line fitting, which meant opening the static system, and did not test it again. Today you plan IFR in Class E airspace. What is true?
options: Legal: the 24 calendar month test is still current
Legal: only the use of a drain valve calls for a new test
Not legal for IFR in controlled airspace until the static system is tested again
Legal if you fly on the alternate static source
questions.why: After any opening and closing of the static system, it must be tested again before IFR in controlled airspace. The only exceptions are using the drain and alternate static valves [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. A current 24-month entry does not cover later work, and using the alternate static source does not cure the opening. A certificated mechanic with an airframe rating may do the static system test [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(b)]].
